HOW TO USE THIS TRACKER — STEP BY STEP

column3: What to Do
column5: Tips

column3: Fill in Project Information on Dashboard: project name, address, type, budget, and target dates
column5: Be specific about your scope. Vague projects get vague bids.

column3: Identify 3–5 contractors to contact. Ask neighbors, check Houzz, Angi, or your local building supply store for referrals
column5: More bids = better comparison. Aim for at least 3.

column3: Enter each contractor's bid details in Bid Comparison: materials, labor, expiry date, timeline, and payment terms
column5: Ask every contractor to break out materials vs. labor — it's easier to compare apples to apples.

column3: Add Total Bid formula in column I (=G+H) so totals calculate automatically
column5: Paste the formula in row 2 then drag it down to row 11.

column3: Check the Expiry Status and Materials Flag columns for automatic alerts
column5: EXPIRING SOON = call the contractor to request an extension before it lapses.

column3: Score each contractor in Contractor Scoring: price is auto-calculated; enter 0–100 for the other four categories
column5: Score these right after each contractor meeting while impressions are fresh.

column3: Review the Weighted Total and Rank columns — the highest-ranked contractor is your top pick on paper
column5: 'Top pick on paper' may not be your gut pick. That's what the Gut Feel score is for.

column3: Call 2–3 references for your top 2 contractors. Log your notes in Reference Check Log
column5: Always ask: 'Would you hire them again?' and 'Is there anything you wish you'd known?'

column3: Verify license and insurance for every contractor you seriously consider. Log results in License & Insurance
column5: Never skip this. An uninsured contractor working on your home = your liability.

column3: Work through all 10 items in the Contract Checklist. Do not sign until every item is verified
column5: If a contractor resists any item on the checklist, that resistance itself is a red flag.

column3: Return to Dashboard and record your final decision: recommended hire, decision date, and notes
column5: File a copy of the signed contract and all COIs in a folder with this tracker.

column3: What to Do Instead

column2: Low bids sometimes mean cut corners on materials, unlicensed subcontractors, or a contractor who underestimates the job and asks for more money mid-project
column3: Use the weighted scoring system to balance price with quality, timeline, and references

column2: If the contractor abandons the job or goes out of business, you lose that money
column3: Structure payments to milestones: 10–15% down, progress payments, 10% retention at completion

column2: Contractors can show expired certificates or list themselves on old policies
column3: Request the Certificate of Insurance be sent directly from the insurance carrier to you

column2: Online reviews can be gamed; direct conversations with past clients cannot
column3: Call at least 2–3 references for any contractor you seriously consider

column2: A one-page contract rarely covers scope, change orders, timeline, or dispute resolution adequately
column3: Use the Contract Checklist to ensure all key terms are in the signed document

column2: Unpermitted work can block your home sale, fail inspection, or void your homeowner's insurance
column3: Verify the contractor will pull permits in their name before any work begins
